newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala exhumation opens painful war wounds.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala exhumation opens painful war wounds.

text.p: Guatemalan forensic scientists have unearthed three bodies in a mass grave of suspected execution victims, opening painful wounds for survivors of the country's 36-year civil war.
Two widows who forced the exhumation have received threats for disturbing the war's buried secrets, Patricia Yoj, attorney for the National Council of Guatemalan Widows, told Reuters on Monday.

"Since they started the exhumation, two women have been threatened," she said. Those who made the threats said "that if at one time they were able to kill 20 or 30 people, they could do so again if the women continue with this."

As in other areas devastated by the long-running war between the goverment and leftist rebels, lingering wounds are pitting neighbour against neighbour in San Andres, an isolated mountain community in the northwestern Quiche province about six hours drive from the Guatemalan capital.

Peace was signed between the two sides last December, but the full story about what happened to the estimated 140,000 people who were killed or disappeared during the conflict is only just beginning to emerge.
Townspeople say that between 250 to 500 civilians were executed from 1980 to 1982 in San Andres, when a ruined local church was taken over by the army and became a killing ground.
"One Good Friday people remember seeing smoke and hearing screams coming from the church," said Celeste Derr, a nun who has lived in the town since 1991.
Now, widows and other survivors go daily to the grave site beneath the floor of the 400-year-old Spanish colonial structure, which has been ruined by earthquakes.
The relatives hope to find their loved ones, give them a Christian burial and punish those responsible for the brutality, said Congresswoman Rosalina Tuyuc, head of the widows' organisation.

Some also blame their neighbours for collaborating with the army during the killings. They claim the neighbours, fearful of being unmasked, are now threatening those who want to get to the truth about the massacres.

The army said it would not make a comment on the affair until a formal complaint was filed, naming names of alleged offenders. "There are lots of groups who make these kinds of accusations," a spokesman said.
On Friday the independent Guatemalan Forensic Anthropology Team uncovered three complete skeletons lying side by side in the first section of an excavation.
"This is clear evidence that people aren't making this up," said anthropologist Fredy A. Peccerelli, a team member.
Maria Uger Chach, 39, keeping vigil with other widows, wept when the skeletons emerged face-up in a bed of red earth.

On Feb. 15, 1981 her 25-year-old husband left their outlying community with his brother and a young neighbour woman to come into town and apply for their identification papers. The three never returned home.
"He owed nothing, had no crime; it was pure evil," she said.
Among those who arrived to help sift through dirt, rocks and bones were a few who had been imprisoned by the army and survived.

Andrea, now 38, followed her husband to the church when he was taken from their home by four soldiers in 1980. She said the soldiers kept her imprisoned for 15 days, during which time they buried her husband before her eyes and repeatedly forced her to perform sex acts.
"I did it to save my life and my children," she said.
She was released and fled to another community, returning to San Andres occasionally to visit her father. Last weekend she pointed out mass grave sites to the forensic team.

The Guatemalan widows' organisation, which petitioned for the exhumation, is seeking protection from police and international observers due to the threats. The United Nations Human Rights Verification Mission in Guatemala (MINUGUA) is investigating, said spokeswoman Valeria Morera.
